summary: This RFC is the official specification of the NICNAME/WHOIS protocol and service, which lets users look up information about people and hosts. It updates RFC 812 and was replaced by RFC 3912.

plainLanguage.summary: You ask a directory, "Who is this?" and it replies with whatever details it has on file.

subtitle: The original WHOIS: connect to TCP port 43, send one line, get a human-readable answer.

tldr.problem: Internet users needed a way to look up people, hosts and organizations registered with the Network Information Center.
tldr.mechanism: A client connects to TCP port 43 on the SRI-NIC host, sends one command line ending in CRLF, reads the reply, and the server closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: It obsoleted RFC 812 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 3912.

today: RFC 954 was obsoleted by RFC 3912, which is now the WHOIS specification to read. It had itself replaced RFC 812.

sections.title: The NICNAME/WHOIS Service
sections.content:
The NICNAME/WHOIS server is a TCP transaction based query/response server running on the SRI-NIC machine. It provides netwide directory service and is one of a series of internet name services maintained by the DDN Network Information Center at SRI International on behalf of the Defense Communications Agency (DCA).

It delivers the full name, U.S. mailing address, telephone number and network mailbox for DDN users registered in the NIC database. It can also look up organizations, DDN nodes and associated hosts, and TAC telephone numbers. The information is delivered in human-readable format.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a phone book for the early network. You ask about a person or computer and it reads back what it knows.

sections.title: The Protocol
sections.content:
The protocol has three steps. Connect to the SRI-NIC service host at TCP port 43 (decimal). Send a single command line ending with CRLF. Receive information in response; the server closes its connection as soon as the output is finished.

User programs are called NICNAME, though many sites use the name WHOIS. Versions existed for TENEX, TOPS-20 and UNIX, and each takes one argument that is passed directly to the server.
sections.plainLanguage: You knock on door number 43, say one sentence, listen to the answer, and the door closes behind it.

sections.title: Command Lines and Replies
sections.content:
A command line is normally a single name specification. Formats will evolve, so sending a lone ? returns the list of formats the server accepts. Replies are not intended to be machine-readable and are meant to go straight to a human.

The help text in the RFC shows several forms. A leading period forces a name-only search and a leading exclamation point forces a handle-only search. Adding ... matches anything from that point. Smith@, @Host and Smith@Host search mailboxes, and a leading asterisk lists the entire membership of a group or host.
sections.plainLanguage: You can type a name, a short nickname, or ask for everyone in a group. Typing a question mark makes the directory explain how to ask.

sections.title: Who Is in the Database
sections.content:
DCA requests that each individual with a directory on an ARPANET or MILNET host, capable of passing traffic across the DoD Internet, be registered in the NIC WHOIS Database. MILNET TAC users must be registered.

Registration is done by sending electronic mail to the NIC registrar with a full name, mailing address, telephone number and one network mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: To be in the phone book you have to send in your name, address and phone number first.

messages.label: Human-readable reply
messages.note: Server closes the connection when output is finished.
